proposals.name: Snatchbats
proposals.entry:
Common Names: Snatchbats, Summer Nicks, Spoonbats
Size: Roughly that of a large housecat
Habitat: Rooftops, chimneys, belfries, attics and dockside warehouses
Season: Appearing chiefly with Fogport's warm summer fogs

Snatchbats are small, winged creatures that arrive in Fogport with the first warm fogs of summer. They are clever, sociable and incurably light-fingered. Open windows attract them. Unlatched cupboards practically constitute an invitation.

A Snatchbat can carry surprising weight, though it flies badly while doing so. Residents commonly see them struggling over the rooftops with tablespoons, candlesticks, boots, hand mirrors, keys or other objects nearly as large as themselves. They prefer items frequently handled by people and show little interest in unattended treasure. A silver spoon used every morning is irresistible; a chest of forgotten coins may go untouched.

Ecology and Habits

Snatchbats arrive in quarrelsome flocks called pilferings. Where they spend the rest of the year is unknown, though sailors claim that summer fogbanks sometimes carry distant chattering voices and the faint clatter of cutlery.

They roost in warm, inaccessible cavities and construct sprawling communal nests from cloth, hair, paper, twine and stolen household goods. Objects are constantly taken from one nest and moved to another, apparently as gifts, challenges or courtship displays. The largest key in a pilfering is usually carried by its dominant member, whether or not the key opens anything.

Their natural diet consists of moths, beetles, fruit, shellfish and the fatty residue skimmed from cookhouse drains. They adore butter, pickled eggs and condensed milk. Feeding them encourages repeat visits and is prohibited under several Civic nuisance ordinances.

Snatchbats rarely attack adults, but they bite when cornered and cooperate vindictively. Anyone striking one may soon discover an entire pilfering outside the bedroom window, throwing roof tiles, pebbles and stolen crockery.

Despite their reputation, they are useful scavengers. They consume enormous numbers of summer insects, recognize individual human faces and can squeeze through openings too small for a person's fist. Rooftop thieves, locksmiths and certain Civic investigators have all attempted to train them—with uneven and usually expensive results.

posts.name: GAMEMASTER SECRETS
posts.entry:
Snatchbats are not merely attracted to shiny objects. They steal things carrying a strong human scent: tools used daily, beloved keepsakes, recently handled evidence and objects clutched during moments of fear. Given several choices, a Snatchbat often takes the object most emotionally important to someone nearby.

This makes their nests accidental archives of Fogport's private lives.

Plot Hooks and Ideas

  • A Snatchbat steals Byl's brass Seventh Foundation token and carries it through an opening no human can enter.
  • Every key in one tenement disappears overnight. The Snatchbats are not building a nest—they are preventing something locked downstairs from being opened.
  • A murder weapon vanishes from Civic custody and appears in a rooftop pilfering. Several innocent people want it found; the murderer wants the entire nest burned.
  • One Snatchbat repeatedly brings Byl gifts stolen from the same unknown woman. The final gift is a bloodstained room key.
  • A wealthy collector offers excellent money for the return of a family signet. The Snatchbats refuse to approach his house and scream whenever they smell him.
  • A pilfering has nested inside the mechanism of a great public clock. Removing them is simple. Removing them without dropping hundreds of stolen valuables onto the crowded street below is not.
  • Snatchbats begin stealing only left shoes from Civic Vigilance officers. Someone has trained them, but not as a joke: the shoes are being used to map patrol assignments by scent.
  • A young Snatchbat becomes attached to Lott and begins “helping” by stealing objects from anyone who argues with him.
  • A nest contains letters from a person believed dead. Some are old, but one was written yesterday.
  • A locksmith secretly keeps trained Snatchbats. They do not pick locks; they steal the original keys and bring them back for copying.
  • A summer pilfering returns carrying unfamiliar coins, military buttons and scraps of foreign uniforms. Something has happened beyond the fog.
  • A Snatchbat steals a Civic pistol and can barely remain airborne. Half the district chases it while the loaded weapon swings from its strap.
  • Someone poisons a pilfering because it nested above a fashionable hotel. Without the Snatchbats, biting summer insects multiply—and something far worse begins using the abandoned roosts.
  • A Snatchbat colony becomes fiercely protective of an apparently worthless spoon. Its hollow handle contains a rolled list of names.
  • A grieving widow feeds the same Snatchbat every evening because it wears her husband's wedding ring around one ankle. It did not take the ring from his home.
  • Children discover that Snatchbats will trade stolen goods for pickled eggs. A thriving schoolyard exchange develops, followed immediately by blackmail, burglary accusations and Civic involvement.
  • A pilfering continually drops keys onto Byl's windowsill. None fit local locks. Arranged by size, however, their teeth form a crude map.
  • A wounded Snatchbat leads the party to a sealed attic filled with generations of stolen belongings—and one very recent captive.
  • Snatchbats suddenly abandon an entire district several hours before each thick fog. They know a predator is coming.
  • An unusually old Snatchbat has learned to imitate several words. It repeats the same address, the word “below,” and Mercy's voice.
